query: What exact annotation conventions will be locked (lesion inclusion/exclusion, min diameter, partial-volume rules), what IRR targets (Dice/Kappa) trigger retraining, and which file formats will be canonical?

response.query: What exact annotation conventions will be locked (lesion inclusion/exclusion, min diameter, partial-volume rules), what IRR targets (Dice/Kappa) trigger retraining, and which file formats will be canonical?
response.answer: Lesion inclusion/exclusion criteria, minimum diameter, and partial-volume rules are defined per IBSI standards. IRR targets of Dice < 0.7 or Kappa < 0.5 trigger retraining. DICOM is the canonical file format.

results.title: [PDF] mint Lesion Radiomics Q&A
results.content: The radiomics features in mint Lesion were developed in accordance with the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI). While radiomics features can be extracted from images as part of routine image analysis, any response criteria in mint Lesion can also be used to capture radiomics information. • Segmentation - ROI delineation (Targets, Non-Targets, etc.), procedure (manually or auto-segmentation) • Interpolation - Voxel dimensions, image interpolation method, image intensity rounding, ROI interpolation method, ROI partial volume • Re-Segmentation - ROI mask criteria • Discretization - Discretization method, discretization parameters • Feature Calculation - Feature set, feature parameters, standardization How did Mint Medical validate the radiomics features?

results.content: # Which of these Q&As about Python return type hints should be the canonical one? The questions to be considered are:. * *How to annotate a generator in Python 3?*. * *How to type hint a generator in Python 3?*. * *What is the return type hint of a generator function?*. * *Proper type annotation of Python functions with yield*. These questions are about the exact same topic, but I think the first one is the best as a duplicate target, since it is the most generic-worded and its answers are the most on-point. ## 1 Answer 1. The first asks the question in a very direct and to-the-point way, and has an appropriate level of generality while still being focused (although I edited out the last sentence for hopefully clear and agreeable reasons). bgusach's answer also gives new, up-to-date information that I don't see on the other questions. It would be even better, arguably, if there were an answer giving clear reasons for when to use the `Iterator` annotation vs `Generator[...]` variants (such as Marcin Orlowski's answer on the second question), but this is already quite good. answered Aug 22 at 3:07. I agree with no comments, and it seems the voters do too, so I've closed the other three questions as a duplicate. While number 3 is technically about doc-strings, the question title will attract people searching for how to write the return type annotation, and the answer is the same anyway. ## You must log in to answer this question. results.title: What file formats will I be working in? – Support
results.content: * When translating file jobs, **text within images is not supposed to be translated**. #### Your translated file Please do not leave the source text together with your translation in your translated file. When you submit your translated file to the customer, it should contain only your translated text (unless the customer specifically requests otherwise, which happens very rarely - for example, an Excel file with columns for both source text and translation). We recently launched a feature that extracts the text from .TXT files and makes it available for translation directly on the workbench. Once you submit your translation, the text will be automatically imported back into a .TXT file for final delivery to the customer.
